### Geographic Distribution

#### Missingness Check
```{python}
# Update these:
eda_table_name = "Unemployment"

# Basic template, needs no changes
with urllib.request.urlopen(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/geojson-counties-fips.json"
    ) as response:
        counties_geojson = json.load(response)

map_df = df[["year", "county_id"]].dropna().copy()

## Get unique years
years = sorted(map_df["year"].dropna().unique())

frames = []

## make one frame per year for time analysis
for year in years:
    df_year = map_df[map_df["year"] == year].copy()

    ## Create df that just checks whether that county has any data
    county_overlay = (
        df_year[["county_id"]]
        .drop_duplicates()
        .assign(has_data = 1)
    )

    ## Create the choropleth overlay
    choropleth = go.Choroplethmap(
        geojson=counties_geojson,
        locations=county_overlay["county_id"],
        z=county_overlay["has_data"],
        featureidkey="id",
        colorscale=[[0, "#fff9f9"], [1, "#2cb94f"]],
        zmin=0,
        zmax=1,
        marker_opacity=0.35,
        marker_line_width=0.3,
        showscale=False,
        hovertemplate="County FIPS: %{location}<br>Has data: Yes<extra></extra>"
    )

    ## Append this year to the frame
    frames.append(
        go.Frame(
            data=[choropleth],
            name=str(int(year))
        )
    )

## Error if there are no years for some reasdon
if not frames:
    raise ValueError(f"No valid yearly data found for {eda_table_name}")

fig = go.Figure(
    data = frames[0].data,
    frames = frames
)
    
## Make it look nice
fig.update_layout(
    title=f"{eda_table_name}: county coverage by year",
    map=dict(
        style="carto-positron",
        center=dict(lat=37.8, lon=-96),
        zoom=3
    ),
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=50, b=0),
    updatemenus=[
        dict(
            type="buttons",
            showactive=False,
            x=0.05,
            y=0.95,
            buttons=[
                dict(
                    label="Play",
                    method="animate",
                    args=[
                        None,
                        {
                            "frame": {"duration": 700, "redraw": True},
                            "transition": {"duration": 300},
                            "fromcurrent": True
                        }
                    ]
                ),
                dict(
                    label="Pause",
                    method="animate",
                    args=[
                        [None],
                        {
                            "frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": False},
                            "transition": {"duration": 0},
                            "mode": "immediate"
                        }
                    ]
                )
            ]
        )
    ],
    sliders=[
        dict(
            active=0,
            currentvalue={"prefix": "Year: "},
            pad={"t": 30},
            steps=[
                dict(
                    label=str(int(y)),
                    method="animate",
                    args=[
                        [str(int(y))],
                        {
                            "frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": True},
                            "transition": {"duration": 0},
                            "mode": "immediate"
                        }
                    ]
                )
                for y in years
            ]
        )
    ]
)

fig.show()
```

#### Values by County

```{python}
# Update these:
eda_table_name = "Unemployment"
cols_to_use = [1,2,3,4]

# Basic template, needs no changes
with urllib.request.urlopen(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/geojson-counties-fips.json"
    ) as response:
        counties_geojson = json.load(response)

## one map per column
for i in cols_to_use:
    value_col = cols[i]
    map_df = df[["year", "county_id", value_col]].dropna().copy()

    ## Get unique years
    years = sorted(map_df["year"].dropna().unique())

    frames = []

    value_min = map_df[value_col].min()
    value_max = map_df[value_col].max()

    ## make one frame per year for time analysis
    for year in years:
        df_year = map_df[map_df["year"] == year].copy()

        ## Create the choropleth overlay
        choropleth = go.Choroplethmap(
            geojson=counties_geojson,
            locations=df_year["county_id"],
            z=df_year[value_col],
            featureidkey="id",
            colorscale="Viridis",
            zmin=value_min,
            zmax=value_max,
            marker_opacity=0.5,
            marker_line_width=0.3,
            colorbar=dict(title=value_col),
            hovertemplate=f"County FIPS: %{{location}}<br>{value_col}: %{{z}}<extra></extra>"
        )

        ## Append this year to the frame
        frames.append(
            go.Frame(
                data=[choropleth],
                name=str(int(year))
            )
        )

    ## Error if there are no years for some reasdon
    if not frames:
        raise ValueError(f"No valid yearly data found for {value_col}")

    fig = go.Figure(
        data = frames[0].data,
        frames = frames
    )
        
    ## Make it look nice
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"{eda_table_name}: {value_col} by county and year",
        map=dict(
            style="carto-positron",
            center=dict(lat=37.8, lon=-96),
            zoom=3
        ),
        margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=50, b=0),
        updatemenus=[
            dict(
                type="buttons",
                showactive=False,
                x=0.05,
                y=0.95,
                buttons=[
                    dict(
                        label="Play",
                        method="animate",
                        args=[
                            None,
                            {
                                "frame": {"duration": 700, "redraw": True},
                                "transition": {"duration": 300},
                                "fromcurrent": True
                            }
                        ]
                    ),
                    dict(
                        label="Pause",
                        method="animate",
                        args=[
                            [None],
                            {
                                "frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": False},
                                "transition": {"duration": 0},
                                "mode": "immediate"
                            }
                        ]
                    )
                ]
            )
        ],
        sliders=[
            dict(
                active=0,
                currentvalue={"prefix": "Year: "},
                pad={"t": 30},
                steps=[
                    dict(
                        label=str(int(y)),
                        method="animate",
                        args=[
                            [str(int(y))],
                            {
                                "frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": True},
                                "transition": {"duration": 0},
                                "mode": "immediate"
                            }
                        ]
                    )
                    for y in years
                ]
            )
        ]
    )

    fig.show()
```

## Summary of Findings

- There are no NA values for any of the columns in this dataset
- The ranges for all value columns are quite high
- The standard deviations of civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed are all more than double the means
- There are no 0 values for any columns in the dataset
- The distributions of all value columns are heavily right-skewed (except for unemployment rate, which is only moderately right-skewed)
- After using a logarithmic scale, civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed are actually extremely normally distributed
- There appears to be high correlation between civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed
- Unemployment rate appears to be only positively correlated with unemployed
- Notably there are missing counties in a few places:
    - One county in SD, which looks like it may be on a reservation
    - A few counties in Virginia, mostly very small but one large one in Norfolk
    - **The ENTIRE state of Louisiana**
- The maps for civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed all look fairly uniform, with large population centers being more lightly colored (higher number)
- The map for unemployment rate is more varied, with some clear geographical trends, such as the middle of the country generally having lower unemployment rates.
